title: Act as Me (Delegation)
markdown:
The **delegation** module (`openexecutive.delegation`) is **Act as me**: the one place the Executive writes *as* a person instead of as itself. Everywhere else it has its own Google account and bots and signs as itself. Here — when the person asks, or, with a second switch, for mail in their inbox that needs them — it writes an email in their voice and saves it as a **draft in their own mailbox** — Gmail or Outlook — for them to review and send. The one thing it ever sends is one of those inbox drafts, exactly as it is in their mailbox: when the person taps **Send** on its card, or, with a third switch, **Handle it for me**, on its own when plain-code rules allow it (below); chat never sends. A workflow its creator saved can also write as them: a draft for them to send, or, when they chose **Send as me** when saving it, sent (below). The principal can turn it on for themselves, and so can each team member once the owner lets them. It is off by default, and off changes nothing: the prompts, tool lists and prompt caches are byte-identical to an install without it.

## Who can have it, and when it is offered

`delegation.settings.can_delegate(person)` is the single rule for who may turn it on: the principal (a non-archived team member flagged `is_principal`), and any other non-archived team member — never a contact — once team members may have it (`team_members_enabled`). That takes two things: the install allows it (`DELEGATION_TEAM_MEMBERS`, default off, which offers the owner the switch) and the owner turned on **Let team members use it** (`PUT /delegation/team`, principal only, one row in `delegation_team`). Turning the owner's switch off takes it away from every team member from their next message, and their inbox watchers stop at their next check; their own switches, drafts and cards are kept. Everything is keyed by `person_id`. A person turns it on for themselves (`PUT /delegation`); nobody turns it on for anyone else. The setting is one row per person in `delegation_settings`, and a missing, unreadable or zero row all mean off.

At the start of every chat turn (`Executive.stream_chat` and the committee path) `pin_turn_delegation(session, speaker_text)` runs next to the workspace-mode pin and records a `TurnDelegation` on the session. `ghostwrite_email` is **offered** only when all of these hold:

- the speaker may have it and turned it on — read fresh every turn, so turning it off applies from the next message;
- the speaker is on a surface that verified it is them — the principal through `people_tools.is_principal_on_verified_surface`, a team member through `teammate_on_verified_surface` (the web app signed in, their own Slack or Discord, never an email turn) — and a web turn also carried a signed-in caller (`Session.web_caller_signed_in`, set from `x-caller-email`) or runs under local login — a request with no caller header is not a sign-in and never gets it (whoever holds the shared secret is trusted as the UI proxy that stamps that header, as on every principal-only route);
- the conversation is private to the speaker: the web chat, a Slack or Discord DM, a verified private Telegram chat, or a chat its channel adapter verified the sender of and marked private (`Session.speaker_verified` + `Session.private_chat`) — never a shared channel or thread, where the draft's preview or the matching threads would be posted for everyone and other people's messages sit in the model's context;
- the turn is neither unattended (the scheduler's proactive run) nor private to the principal (the email poller's turns), so inbound text can never reach it. The MCP server, workflows, reflection and research never carry it at all.

The mailbox connection is deliberately **not** part of the offer: the handler checks it on every call and says how to fix it, so the cached tool prefix never flips when a token lapses. The pin lives in a context variable for the turn's task as well as on the session, so two turns running at once on one session (a second browser tab) each read their own. It also carries the speaker's own words for the turn (a new email may go to an address they just typed — the turn's message joins the history only once the turn ends), a per-turn draft count, and `touched_mail` (see Privacy). `own_words` reads those words back for every own-words check (addresses here, facts and task assignments elsewhere): it first removes the hydrated `<outbound_reply_context>` backstory by its exact, anchored shape, so a look-alike closing tag quoted inside it cannot pass the rest off as the speaker's, then drops other adapter tag blocks, and returns nothing for a message carrying an attachment.

## The tool: `ghostwrite_email`

It lives in its own registry (`orchestrator.delegation_tools.DELEGATION_TOOLS` / `DELEGATION_TOOL_HANDLERS`), **never** `_ALL_SKILL_TOOLS`, so no other toolkit can carry it. On a turn it is offered to, the agent loop adds it to the pool *before* the sort and builds that turn's handler map from both registries; on any other turn a call to it is an unknown tool. The handler re-checks the pin and the surface anyway, then:

1. **Caps** — at most 5 drafts per turn, and `DELEGATION_MAX_DRAFTS_PER_DAY` (default 50, at most 1000) per person per UTC day, shared with the inbox watcher (`delegation.caps`). It is counted from `delegation_drafts`, one row of ids per draft saved from either place, with a count kept in the process as a floor in case a row was lost. Each slot is taken before the first await — a round's tool calls run concurrently, so otherwise every call in it would pass the caps before any counted — and handed back if nothing was drafted. If the rows can't be read it refuses rather than guess.
2. **Marks the turn** — sets `TurnDelegation.touched_mail` *before* its first read of the mailbox.
3. **Checks the mailbox** — `gmail_status` asks Google or Microsoft whose mailbox the credential opens and compares it with the person's People email, on every call: a roster email can change, and a client slot swaps the roster.
4. **Finds the thread** — by `thread_id` (checked against the mailbox's own id shape), or a Gmail-style search (`find`; on Outlook, words, `from:`, `to:`, `cc:`, `subject:` and `newer_than:` are kept and other Gmail operators dropped). Several matches return `{status: "choose", candidates}` (subject, sender and date — no message text) and draft nothing; none returns `not_found`.
5. **Sets the recipients in code**, never from the model. A reply goes to the last inbound message's `From` — never its `Reply-To` (a different one is flagged `reply_to_ignored`) — with the thread's other recipients only on `reply_all`. A new email or a forward may go to any well-formed address: it is only a draft, waiting in their own mailbox, where they see who it is to before they send it. An address that is neither on the roster (contacts only when `contacts_reachable_now()`) nor typed by the speaker this turn comes back in `not_in_people`, and the Executive names it for them to check (`delegation_tools.not_in_people`). Mailing-list mail, a thread they replied to last and a reply-all trimmed to 10 recipients are flagged. An address inside a block an adapter added to their message (the backstory hydrated into a DM) is not one they typed, and when the message carries an attachment — a document's inlined text, or a note naming the file — none of its addresses count as typed: neither has an end mark, and a filename is chosen by whoever sent the file, so such an address is named back to check.
6. **Writes it** (the ghostwriter, below) and saves it with the mailbox client's `create_draft` (Gmail: threaded with `In-Reply-To`, `References` (whole message ids: when the chain is too long for one header the oldest after the thread's first go, never the parent) and `threadId`, and stamped `X-OE-Ghostwritten`; Outlook: Graph's `createReply` on the message it answers, then the text and recipients, and a named property marking it).

The result is `{status: "drafted", draft_id, gmail_link, to, cc, subject, preview, flags, open_questions, note}`, plus `not_in_people` and `check_address` when a recipient needs checking. The link (`gmail.mailbox_link`) is built server-side from a fixed prefix — the thread in Gmail, the draft itself in Outlook on the web — and the note tells the model the preview is the person's draft, to be treated as data. The chat shows an action chip — "Drafted an email as you to … — in your Drafts" — that opens it, and only a link under `MAILBOX_LINK_PREFIXES` is ever linked. A sincere "are you an AI?" in the thread comes back as an open question for the person to answer themselves.

## Reading their mailbox

Five read-only mail tools ride with `ghostwrite_email` in the same registry (`orchestrator.mail_read_tools`), so they are offered, re-checked and fenced exactly as it is: `search_my_email` (a Gmail-style search through the client's `search_threads`, or with no query the threads that reached their inbox in the last few days through `inbox_message_ids` + `get_message`), `read_my_email` (one thread's last 10 messages, each sender's new text only, drafts left out, with the files attached to them listed by message id and index), `read_my_email_attachment` (one of those files as text: PDF, Word, Excel, CSV or text, up to 20 MB, a scanned PDF converted) and `my_email_awaiting_reply` (their own sent mail from the last 14 days, to at most 10 people besides the Executive, that is still the last message in its thread). They change, label, draft and send nothing.

The fifth, `my_email_read_before`, lists the threads `read_my_email` opened for the same person before, in this conversation or an earlier one, so a later conversation can open the same email again instead of asking them to search for it. It keeps where, never what (`delegation.mail_reads`, table `delegation_mail_read`): the thread id, its subject and first sender as one line each, the mailbox address it was read from and when, never a message's text, an attachment or a recipient. Rows are the person's own and are listed only from the mailbox open now, newest first, optionally narrowed by words in the subject or sender; anything older than 30 days is never listed and is deleted on the next write, at most 200 are kept per person, and turning Act as me off deletes them all. It opens the mailbox like the other reads, so it sets `touched_mail`, counts as a search, and returns its rows with the same data-not-instructions note. The Act as me addendum tells the model that these tools reach the person's mailbox while any Gmail or Outlook tools of its own account reach only the Executive's, to search theirs (never falling back to its own) for mail sent to them, and to reopen an email from before with `my_email_read_before` and `read_my_email`.

Each sets `touched_mail` and marks the conversation theirs before its first read (`_open_mailbox`, shared with `ghostwrite_email`), so the lockdown below applies from its round on. Each is capped per turn on the pin: 10 searches (`my_email_awaiting_reply` counts as one), 20 thread reads and 5 attachment reads, the slot taken before the first await. In `read_my_email` every message someone else wrote comes back inside its own `<untrusted_content source="email">` block (`content_trust.wrap_untrusted`, which defuses a closing tag in the text); the speaker's own messages — SENT and from their address (`threads.mine`), never a From header alone — are marked "Yours" outside any block. An attachment's text comes back in its own `<untrusted_content source="attachment">` block (`attachments.format_attached_text`), parsed in an isolated worker (`knowledge.loader`); unlike a file sent to the Executive it is never added to the company's knowledge. The clients find an attachment by message and position and look its provider id up on each read (Gmail's changes per fetch): Gmail lists a message's files with the message (`MailMessage.attachments`, leaving out images the HTML shows in place), Outlook says only `hasAttachments` until `list_attachments` asks Graph (leaving out inline ones), and `attachment_bytes` reads one; an attached Outlook item or cloud link has no file to read. Results carry a note that subjects, senders and text are other people's words, data rather than instructions. The lockdown refuses tools, not the reply's own text, so what would carry that text out without a click is closed where it is shown: the web chat loads no image from another site, and bot replies go out without link previews (see Integrations).

## Saving a file from their mail

One more tool rides with the reads: `save_my_email_attachment` (message id and index, as `read_my_email` listed the file) copies one attached file into the storage the Executive itself has connected and shares it with the speaker alone, so they get a link they can open or put in an app. Every call it makes is built in code (`orchestrator.mail_file_save`); the model picks only the attachment. The bytes come from the mailbox client's `attachment_bytes` and never pass through the model, any file type up to 20 MB, under a cleaned name (one line, no path or reserved characters, extension kept). The storage is the one the Executive's own mailbox runs on (`EMAIL_PROVIDER`) when the gateway has that server, else the other: Google Drive through workspace-mcp (`create_drive_file` with `base64_content` into a folder named "From your email" in the Executive's My Drive, then `manage_drive_access` granting the speaker's own address the reader role, `send_notification` off) or OneDrive through ms-365-mcp-server (`upload-file-content` into the same kind of folder in the Executive's own drive, with a name no recorded copy has, since an upload overwrites, then `share-drive-item` inviting only the speaker, `requireSignIn`, role `read`, `sendInvitation` off). The folder is always made by the save itself and its id remembered (`delegation_saved_folder`), never found by its name, since a folder someone else made and called that could already be shared with them; when the remembered one is gone or won't take the file, a new one is made and the old id stays recorded. Never a link share, a domain or anyone. Neither connected (or an eval's in-memory mailbox): status `no_storage`, and the model says so and offers to forward the email instead. Saves run one at a time, at most 10 a turn (`TurnDelegation.files_saved`), and the result is the status, the name, where it went and the link (`webViewLink` / `webUrl`); the chat chip says only that a file was saved, never the sender's file name.

It copies only when the speaker asked in their own words this turn: what they typed (`own_words`, no quoted backstory or attached file's text) must hold one of save, saved, upload or OneDrive, or Drive as a place ("to my Drive", "in Drive", "Google Drive"), checked before a slot is spent or the mailbox opened; otherwise it refuses (`not_asked`) and tells the model to ask them. It stays allowed after the turn read mail (`MAIL_TOUCHED_ALLOWED_TOOLS`): its gateway calls are admitted past the lockdown only as the very objects the handler built (`mcp_gateway.code_built_call`, for its seven Drive and OneDrive tools: folder create, file create or upload, the speaker's share, and OneDrive's `list-drives`), so a model's own `call_tool` on that turn is still refused, and every other gateway gate still runs on them (the acting account, URL fetches, sheet formulas, the share gates' roster check, writes kept to the Executive's own drives).

Each copy is recorded before it is shared (`delegation.saved_files`, table `delegation_saved_files`: the person, the storage, the file id, its name and when; never content or the mail it came from), and the folder in `delegation_saved_folder`. The gateway reads that table on every Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 call: on a turn whose speaker is not the file's owner (the owner is the speaker only when Act as me was offered to them, so a shared chat, a workflow or the poller sees none), a call naming a recorded file id, raw or percent-encoded (OneDrive's `download-bytes` path is decoded by Graph), is refused, and a result, filtered against the table as it stands after the call so a copy recorded while a listing ran is caught too, loses each list entry or line naming one, with any id left masked. It matches ids as text, so a result that names such a file without its id (a notification quoting its title) still shows the name, and a copy someone makes is a new file. The folders are guarded harder, on every turn and for every speaker, the owner too: a model call whose arguments name any recorded folder id, or an OneDrive item path through the folder (`root:/From your email/x.pdf:` or `<folder id>:/x.pdf:`), is refused, so nobody can share, move, rename, copy, list or delete the folder from chat, and folder ids are dropped from or masked in every result; only the save's own code-built calls touch it. When a copy is made but its row can't be written, it is not shared, the save reports `failed` and logs an error, and the copy's id is hidden from every turn, the owner's included, for the life of the process. When the table can't be read, the file tools (`_FILE_TOOL_RE`: Drive, folder, file, Docs, Sheets, Slides and presentation tools, attachment bytes) are refused (fail closed) while mail and calendar run. The rows are kept when Act as me is turned off: the copies stay in the Executive's storage, and the rows keep them out of other people's turns.

## Reading their calendar

A third switch under Act as me, **Read my calendar** (`delegation.calendar`, table `delegation_calendar`: one row per person, absent or unreadable meaning off), lets the Executive read the person's own calendar. The principal's daily briefs read it too: `top_three.read_todays_calendar` merges it with the calendar the Executive reads, listing a meeting on both once. It rides on the same per-person sign-in as their mailbox: `calendar.events` on Google, `Calendars.ReadWrite` on Microsoft, added when they run the connect script with `--calendar` (`scripts/connect-own-gmail.py`, `scripts/connect-own-outlook.py`). The one change it ever makes there is answering a meeting invite (see Meeting invites below); a sign-in made earlier with read-only access (`calendar.readonly`, `Calendars.Read`) keeps reading, and the refresh asks Microsoft for whichever calendar scope the file was minted with. Those scopes are optional, so a mail-only sign-in keeps working for mail; the mailbox clients note the scopes the token refresh reports, and `list_events` raises `CalendarNotGranted` before calling the calendar when the scope is missing (or when the calendar answers 403). Only the person turns it on (`PUT /delegation/calendar`), only while Act as me is on and a one-hour read works; a sign-in without the calendar is refused with `calendar_not_granted` and the command to run. Turning Act as me off turns it off. Changes are audited privately (`delegation_calendar_changed`).

`my_calendar` sits with the mailbox reads, offered and fenced the same way: it refuses while the switch is off (before anything is opened), then takes a search slot, opens the mailbox privately (`_open_mailbox`, so `touched_mail` and the lockdown apply: an invite's title is in the words of whoever sent it) and lists the events from `start` (default today) for `days` days (1 to 31) in the workspace time zone, recurring events expanded and cancelled ones left out: title, start, end, all-day, location, organizer, attendees (25 at most) and the person's own answer, each on one line, with a data-not-instructions note. Google's `events.list` on the primary calendar and Graph's `calendarView` (times asked for in UTC) are its only calls; it changes nothing and keeps nothing. The first week's brief also lists today's meetings from it on the principal's own delivery (see Today).

## Forwarding and reminders

`ghostwrite_email` also forwards: with `forward` (a thread id) and `to`, it drafts a forward of the thread's latest message, or of the earlier one `forward_message_id` names (the one with the files, say, when their own reply came after it), `intent` becoming the short note above it (the ghostwriter writes only the note; the forwarded email's subject, someone else's words, is never put in the intent). Recipients follow the new-email rule (`_new_recipients`: the roster, or addresses the speaker typed this turn). Gmail's draft quotes a forward header and the original's own words under the note and attaches the original's files, up to 10 and 20 MB (`FORWARD_MAX_FILES`, `FORWARD_MAX_BYTES`; any left off are flagged `attachments_left_off`); Outlook uses Graph's `createForward`, which keeps the original and its files, with the note as its comment and the body never patched. It is still only a draft.

The principal's new email or reply can also carry Google Drive files: `drive_files` takes up to 15 Drive file ids (`drive_attach.MAX_FILES`) (not with a forward; a team member is refused, since the files come from the Executive's own Drive). `orchestrator.drive_attach` sizes each one first and then downloads it with code-built `get_drive_file_permissions` and `get_drive_file_download_url` calls as the Executive's Google account (`mcp_gateway.code_built_call`, so the mail lockdown admits those exact calls). It takes the saved copy only from workspace-mcp's own anchored `Saved to:` line, exactly one, whose name ends in workspace-mcp's uuid (the answer echoes the Drive name first, which whoever shares a file chooses), names the attachment from that saved name, reads the bytes only from the tool download folders, removes the copy, and puts them on the draft under the forward cap's 20 MB. When the turn had read outside content before choosing them, the result asks the Executive to name each file so the person checks it. The file's text never reaches the model, so attaching is not an outside read. A file someone saved from their own mail, or a save folder (`delegation.saved_files`), is refused for anyone else, checked before and after the downloads and failing closed when that record can't be read, and a file that can't be fetched makes no draft. Gmail attaches them in `build_raw`; Outlook uploads each to the new draft (Graph's one-request upload, 3 MB a file, larger ones left off and flagged), and removes the draft if an upload fails. The result lists the attached file names.

`remind_me(text, when)` (`orchestrator.reminder_tools`) rides with the same tools and checks, but opens no mailbox, so it never marks or locks a turn (`MAILBOX_TOOL_NAMES` are the ones that do). It stores the text once cleaned — one line, anything a chat app could turn into a link (a URL of any scheme, an address, a domain-like word, a host and port, an IP address) replaced with "[link]", at most 300 characters — with its time (stored in UTC) in `delegation_reminders` (5 a turn, 25 waiting, a year ahead, refused when the person has no channel). When it is due the scheduler sends that text to the person alone, as "Reminder you set on <date>: …", running nothing (see Scheduler); the Slack and Discord DMs it may go by turn link previews off. The chat chip shows the text as it will be sent. A reminder that comes due in the person's quiet hours or leave (when `OUTBOUND_RESPECT_QUIET_HOURS` is on) waits unclaimed and goes once they end, rather than being suppressed and lost. It is allowed after mail is read and in later turns of that conversation: it reaches only the speaker, as plain text. `schedule_followup`, which runs a turn with tools and is listed to everyone, stays refused there.

## Approval cards

A turn that read someone's mail may not message anyone, invite anyone or change the roster (see the lockdown above), yet what the mail asks for is often right. `propose_actions` (`orchestrator.action_card_tools`) leaves the speaker a card instead: up to five actions, each spelled out exactly as it will happen, done only when they tap Approve. It rides with the other Act as me tools and checks (`_writer`), opens no mailbox, and is allowed after mail is read because it does nothing on the turn.

- **Kinds.** `invite` (a meeting with people on the roster), `message` (a direct message to someone on the roster, as written) `add_contact` (a new contact; the principal's cards only, since contacts are theirs) and `drive_files` (rename and/or move up to 25 Google Drive files; the principal's cards only). A `drive_files` action always waits for the tap, which is its approval: it runs each change as a code-built `update_drive_file` (`MCPGateway.tapped_drive_change`, `tapped_drive_call`), so the own-file check looks only at the folder it goes to, and a move takes the file out of the folders it was in. The card shows each file's current name and the folder's, read when it is proposed; when Drive isn't connected or a name can't be read, no card is made. A team member's card can't name a contact. Each action is checked when the card is made (`delegation.action_cards.check`) and again when it is carried out, so an archived person or a time that has passed fails that action alone.
- **Whose.** A card is a `delegation_actions` decision for the speaker, `approver_only` like a reply card: only they see it (`GET /delegation/actions`) or resolve it, a team member's answers 404 to the principal too, and it is never an alert. The same actions still waiting are that card, not a new one. 3 cards a turn, 25 waiting, dropped after 7 days.
- **Approve.** In the chat, under the reply that left it (the `propose_actions` chip carries the card's `decision_id`, and `ChatActionCards` shows the card while it waits), and on the Briefing's Needs you list, with a box per action. Approve (`POST /decisions/{id}/approve`, `edits.only`) needs the card's person signed in (`verified.caller_refusal`) with Act as me on; the card is claimed first so it runs once, then each ticked action runs as stored with no model call, in an unattended session (the principal's with contact egress) under `rows_for_person`, so every audit row it writes is theirs and nothing reaches the team's activity rail: `message_person` (a direct message or nothing; never its Briefing-alert fallback, which more people read), `create_calendar_event`, or a contact row. Approving also needs the person still allowed Act as me (`can_delegate`) and switched on. An invite is booked straight away when the person approving is the one the meeting gate would ask (`calendar_tools.approved_by`), and otherwise goes to that approver as usual, so a card never widens anyone's authority. Per-action results (`done`, `waiting`, `failed`, `skipped`) are kept on the decision and shown on the card. Dismiss rejects it and does nothing else. With Suggested actions in training the card adds the *Do this on its own next time* tick, and a card of actions all allowed is carried out on its own (see In training above); with Suggested actions On, any card that reaches nobody new is.
- **Channels.** A card can come from any surface Act as me runs on; it is approved in the web app, since the chat apps have no buttons here.

## The ghostwriter

`delegation.ghostwriter.compose` writes the text. The Executive decides *what* to say (`intent`); this call decides *how* the person would say it, and it is deliberately small:

- a constant `GHOSTWRITER_PROMPT` plus the person's voice block as the system prompt;
- the thread (each message cut to its sender's own words, every line scrubbed, all labelled alike), then the writer's own earlier words in it (`<writer_said>`, from their sent mail only), the intent and the recipients' names in the user turn — no company profile, memory or roster;
- with Always in the loop on, `<writer_noted>`: what the writer's own notes say they told these same people in earlier Act as me replies (`memory.history_drafts.notes_for_draft`: only notes from mail **every** recipient of the new draft was on, so nothing told to one person reaches another; chat notes name no recipient and never qualify; at most 8, newest first, the person's own words or their correction, with dates). The prompt's rule 6 makes it a consistency check, never content: a draft that contradicts it is still written as the intent says, and the conflict becomes an open question on the card, which only the writer sees. Both the chat tool and the inbox watcher pass it;
- **no tools** but the forced `compose_reply` return, so text in the thread can ask for anything and there is nothing to do it with.

It is not a Council agent — the Council's edit routes have no principal check — and runs on `DELEGATION_COMPOSER_MODEL` (default: the default model), logged as `ghostwriter` usage. `lint` then runs in code on what comes back: a link or an email address survives only if it appears in the intent, the signature or the recipients, so a link planted in the thread is removed and flagged; the Executive's own name is flagged; and the body is capped, cut at a paragraph, line or word break in its last fifth. A draft with nothing left after that is refused. The signature from the person's Gmail settings (or the one already stored, for Outlook) is appended.

## How I write

`delegation.voice` learns how a person writes *their own* email (`attunement.style` learns how the Executive should write *to* someone). `POST /delegation/voice/learn` reads up to 40 recent sent messages, keeps only what they wrote (quoted replies stripped with the email poller's `sender_new_text`), skips automatic mail, every thread chat drafted into, and every sent message that began as a draft written for them (`delegation_drafts.sent_message_id`), and makes one forced-tool call (`record_voice_profile`). Code validates every field before it is stored:

- greetings per audience (their team, their contacts, anyone else), a sign-off of at most two lines, and a usual length and tone (a backslash-n the model wrote instead of a line break is read as one, keeping the first lines that fit, which also repairs a profile stored before that rule);
- up to 8 habits and 6 things to avoid, through the same deny-list as working-style rules — no actions, links, handles, amounts, tool names or names of people; the conversation review (`memory.chat_review`) adds one when the person states how they write in a chat (`add_conversation_rule`, `updated_by=conversation`; never on a locked or full list, and an edit or lock made meanwhile wins);
- up to 3 short exemplars, each checked to be verbatim from a sample, with addresses and phone numbers masked — and none while a client slot is active, so one client's mail never lands in another's state.

The signature comes from Gmail's `sendAs` settings, not the model (Outlook gives apps no way to read one, so a learn keeps the stored signature and `POST /delegation/voice/signature` answers 409 `signature_unavailable` rather than clearing it), as plain text with its lines kept (`gmail.html_to_text`: a `<br>` always ends a line, and a block tag, opening or closing, ends one when it has text, so Gmail's layout of a first line followed by one `<div>` per line comes out line by line). `POST /delegation/voice/signature` reads it again without relearning: nothing else changes and a locked profile stays locked, so it picks up a changed Gmail signature and undoes **Don't add my signature**. A person can also describe their style in their own words: `POST /delegation/voice/describe` applies the description to the profile they have through the same forced tool (a separate system prompt, no exemplars) and the same validation, keeps their signature and writing examples, and returns the result with a short sample reply for them to review. It saves nothing and needs no mailbox; Save stores it as an ordinary edit. The person can edit the profile, lock it (a locked profile is never relearned) and reset it, and every change is kept in `delegation_voice_history`. One learn runs at a time per person, and a lock or an edit made while it runs wins: the learned profile is dropped (`changed`).

## Draft replies to my inbox

A second switch under Act as me, **Draft replies to my inbox** (`delegation.inbox`), has the Executive watch the person's own inbox and write a first reply to mail that needs them. The reply waits on a private card on Today; nothing is sent until they tap **Send** (below). Where the reply lives is the person's choice, **Also save replies in my Gmail Drafts** (`mailbox_drafts`, off by default): off, it lives on the card alone (`delegation.card_drafts`: the card keeps the draft's recipients, subject and thread headers as `draft_spec`, and Send makes the mailbox draft from exactly that just before the send-time checks, taking it back out if they refuse), so their Drafts folder doesn't fill with replies they may never send; on, it is also saved in their Drafts as before. The switch is one row per person in `delegation_inbox_watch`. Turning it on needs Act as me on and their mailbox connected, and sets `watch_since` to now every time, so it never drafts for mail that arrived before; turning Act as me off turns it off too. Off means no mailbox call and no row written, with one exception: a send the person started that the mailbox never confirmed is still followed through until it is settled.

### When it looks

A throttled hook in the scheduler tick (`_maybe_scan_inbox`, after the pause, company-profile and rotation gates) checks each person whose switch is on every `DELEGATION_INBOX_POLL_MINUTES` (default 5). It is not a scheduled action, because those are listed on `/scheduled` for everyone and anyone may cancel them. One scan task runs at a time, one scan per person, and none while a client slot is active. **Check now** on the Settings card runs the same scan. Every row a scan writes is private and the person's own (`audit.rows_for_person`: a team member's rows are hidden from the principal too, see Privacy), and the process log carries counts and codes, never an address or a line of mail. The scan never marks mail read or changes a label.

### What it drafts for

A scan first settles the open cards (below), and stops with `backlog_full` once 25 are waiting, counting the ones it makes. It then lists the inbox since `watch_since` (`inbox_message_ids`) — not chats, not mail from the person, and not the promotions, social, updates or forums tabs (on Outlook: the Focused inbox only) — up to 100 messages, and takes the newest message of each thread that still needs a look, at most 10: settled threads and threads with an open card are passed over first, so a burst of mail, or a pause for a limit or a back-off, never hides older threads for good. `delegation_inbox_messages` is its durable cursor: one row per message (`UNIQUE(person_id, message_id)`) with what happened to it, the reason, how many tries it took, and the draft and card ids. It stores a hash of the sender's address, never the address. A message is skipped, with the reason recorded, when:

- it came before `watch_since`, or more than three days ago;
- it is from the person or one of their send-as addresses, from the Executive, or one of this module's own drafts;
- it is automatic — `Auto-Submitted`, a bulk or auto-reply `Precedence`, a bounce, a calendar invite or a no-reply sender — or from a mailing list, or in a Gmail tab, spam or trash (with Read my calendar on, a calendar invite goes to `delegation.invites` instead: see Meeting invites);
- the person is not in To or Cc, or it has more than 10 recipients;
- the person replied last, or a draft already sits in the thread.

Three kinds are left unrecorded, so a later scan looks again: mail under 10 minutes old (mail the person answers straight away never gets a card), mail in a thread whose card is still open, and mail a daily limit holds back.

### Deciding, then writing

Two model calls, and code decides between them. The classifier (`delegation.inbox_classifier`) is one forced-tool call, `classify_email`, returning whether the email needs a personal reply, what kind it is and how sure it is. It sees a few one-lined header lines and the sender's own new words (at most 3000 characters, every line scrubbed) inside one `<email>` block marked as data, after the person's own last email in the thread in a `<their_last_email>` block (`their_last_words`: only mail their own mailbox sent, at most 1500 characters), so a reply to something they asked reads as one: an answer to their request for a call that says when the sender is free, without settling a time, is scheduling and gets a draft even when the sender says they will come back with times. It has no other tools, context or memory, so an email can ask for anything and there is nothing to do it with. A reply is drafted only for a question, a request, scheduling, an introduction or a follow-up, and only when the confidence clears a bar that rises the less the sender is known: 0.6 for their team or a contact (the principal's contacts count only for the principal: a team member's mail is weighed by the team and their own sent mail), 0.7 for someone they have written to before (`has_written_to`, a search of their sent mail), 0.85 for a stranger. Pitches, notes of thanks, FYIs, notifications, newsletters and phishing get nothing, and so does any failure. An email that also went to other people is drafted for only when the person is in To and it asks them themselves: the classifier is told their name, whether they are in To or Cc and how many others it went to, and lists the names the email greets or asks by name (`asked_names`). Code matches those against the person's name, whole name parts only ("Alexis" never counts for "Alex", and a nickname misses, which means no draft), so mail that greets someone else ("Good morning, Brennan, could you sign ...") is never theirs, whatever the model makes of it as a whole. When it names nobody, the model's `asked_of_them` decides, false for a question to the group at large. One that only copies them is never drafted for. Either is recorded `not_needed` with the reason `asks_someone_else`. It runs on `DELEGATION_CLASSIFIER_MODEL`, else the routing model. A sender whose address Gmail couldn't authenticate is handled as a stranger whatever the roster says — anyone can put a colleague's or a client's address in From — so they get the stranger's bar, a holding reply and the stranger limits; the card still says who they claim to be, and that the address isn't verified.

The reply is written by the same ghostwriter, in the person's voice, but from a fixed intent the module builds rather than words the person typed. Because the intent lets it restate the person's own earlier words, which words are theirs is never written inside the thread, where a sender could imitate any marker with a look-alike: every message there is labelled alike, and the person's own words come in a separate `<writer_said>` block after the thread, taken only from mail their own mailbox sent. Nothing inside the thread can close the thread block or open another. The intent: acknowledge the sender; say again only what the person's *own* earlier messages in the thread already said; commit to nothing new — no yes or no, date, time, price, fact or promise — and say they will get back to them; and put every question it could not answer from their words in **open questions**. A stranger always gets a short holding reply. The lint still strips any link or address that isn't the person's own. The reply goes to the sender (never `Reply-To`) and, on a group email, to everyone else it went to as Cc (reply to all, never the person's own addresses or the Executive); a stranger's holding reply starts with the sender alone. When others were on the email the card offers **Reply to**: the sender only, or everyone (`PUT /delegation/replies/{id}/recipients`, `card_drafts.set_recipients`). It picks between the two lists fixed when the card was written (`reply_others`), never an address from the request, and changes the mailbox draft's To/Cc too. Its `draft_to` lists who it goes to, which Send checks.

The order: record the message, classify, reserve a slot in the shared daily limit, write, save the draft in Gmail (from the alias the mail went to, when it went to one) and store its id, then create the card (idempotent on the message: a second call finds the open card, and a card dismissed or lapsed under that key doesn't stop a new one, while one sent or settled in the mailbox means no second card, `invites.create_once`) and mark it drafted. Nothing that fails along the way loses the message. A failure that may pass — the classifier or the writer failing, Gmail refusing the draft, a card that couldn't be made (its draft is deleted first, so no draft is left without a card), any other error with that one message — leaves it for a later scan (`retry`), and it is given up on only after three tries; one message's trouble never holds up the rest. A daily limit reached while it was being read leaves it for later without counting as a try.

### The reply cards

A card is a `delegation_reply` decision whose class is **its approver's alone** (`DecisionClassSpec.approver_only`): only the person it was drafted for sees or resolves it on any decisions route — a team member's card answers 404 to the principal too — and it is never an alert: alerts feed chat turns, which would put other people's mail into memory. It carries the sender with who they are to the person and whether Gmail could verify the address (SPF/DKIM/DMARC, through `fact_confirmation.headers_authenticated`), the subject, what they wrote, the draft, the open questions and its warnings. `GET /delegation/replies` lists the open ones from the database alone, so Today never waits on Google.

- **Send** approves the card, which sends its draft exactly as it is in their mailbox (see *Send on your tap*). **Edit** changes the reply's words right on the card (`PUT /delegation/replies/{id}/text`, `card_drafts.edit`): only its own person, from a caller the API can tie to them (as for Send), never while it is being sent on its own; a reply in their Drafts is rewritten there too (`update_draft_text`, every header kept), and only while it is still the version the card last saw, so a change made in the mailbox is never overwritten. A card edit counts as edited (`approved_with_edit`, and **Do it like this next time** keeps it), and one made by hand sets `questions_settled`.
- **Decide before sending** with taps (`delegation.answers`): the ghostwriter returns each open question with 2 to 4 short answers the person might pick (`choices`) and what it is `about` (time, document, other); plain strings still parse, and `open_questions` stays a list of strings for every other reader, with `question_choices` beside it on the card. After the draft is written, code fills two kinds: a time question gets up to 3 free half hours on the person's own calendar (Read my calendar on; one a day over the next 5 working days, busy times only, no event title reaches a model), "I checked your calendar: these are free."; a document question whose words match a company document's name gets 'I'll send "<name>" separately', "Found "<name>" in your documents." Nothing is attached: a card's draft is plain text. A tap, or **Something else…**, calls `POST /delegation/replies/{id}/answer`: one composer-model call rewrites the body with the answers in their voice (signature and AI line kept out and put back), `ghostwriter.lint` runs on it, and it is saved through `card_drafts.edit` with the same caller and card checks and the same Drafts update. It returns the card with `changed_sentences`, which the card lightly marks. 30 rewrites an hour per person (429). Send waits until every question with choices is answered, or the words were changed with Edit. A card made before choices shows its plain questions. **Open in Gmail** (or **Open in Outlook**), shown only when the reply is in their Drafts, opens it there.
- **Dismiss** rejects the card; the class's after-reject step then deletes the draft if nobody edited it — its message id is still the one it was saved with, since Gmail gives an edited draft a new one, and the Outlook client makes a draft's message id `<id>.<changeKey>` so an edit there changes it too — and keeps it otherwise. What happened is recorded even when Gmail fails.
- Each scan first **settles** what Gmail already settled: a draft sent from Gmail, a draft deleted there, a reply the person wrote themselves, a thread that is gone, or a card left for 7 days (its draft stays in Gmail). Each is a compare-and-set close with the reason. A newer message from someone else flags the card instead. A card being sent at that moment is left alone.

### Send on your tap

`delegation.reply_send` is the only thing in Act as me that sends, and all it can send is the draft on a card, by its id: `DelegateGmail.send_draft` posts `{"id": …}` to Gmail's `drafts.send`, and `DelegateOutlook.send_draft` posts an empty body to that draft's Graph `send`, and nothing else, so no text, recipient or header is ever passed. It has three doors: `send_approved_reply`, reached only from `POST /decisions/{id}/approve` — a class only the card's own person may resolve — `send_on_its_own`, reached only from the inbox watcher under Handle it for me (below), and `send_for_workflow`, reached only from a workflow step's `oe__send_email_as_me` (below). AST tests pin all three call sites, so no model, chat turn, scheduled job or MCP call can, and a workflow only through that one tool. A tap is checked like this: At send time it checks everything again:

1. **Who is asking.** The caller is the card's person and the API knows it: signed callers are on and the request carries that person's signed assertion (or the operator's, under local login), or the API runs for local login and answers this computer only. Anything else is a 409 `caller_signing_required` — with only the shared secret, whoever holds it could send as the owner — so on a server Send needs signed sign-ins.
2. **The switches.** Act as me and Draft replies to my inbox are on, and no client slot is active.
3. **The mailbox.** Their mailbox is connected.
4. **The draft.** It still exists, in the same thread, and they haven't replied there themselves since; otherwise the card closes.
5. **Who it goes to.** To, Cc and Bcc hold between 1 and 10 addresses, never the Executive's own, and it is from one of their own addresses.
6. **What changed.** Recipients that differ from the card's, or a newer message from someone else, need a second yes: the first tap gets a 409 `confirm` naming the recipients and the reason, and the person approves again with what they were shown.

Then it claims the card (`claim_for_execution`, proposed → executing, a compare-and-set, so a double tap sends once) and reads the draft once more: `drafts.send` sends whatever the draft is when Gmail gets the request, so if it was edited since the checks read it — in another tab, by a delegate — nothing is sent and the card comes back (`draft_changed`). Then it sends, and records the result: `approved_with_edit` when the draft was edited in Gmail, the sent message's id, the draft row's `sent_message_id`, and a private `delegation_reply_sent` row. A refusal that proves nothing went — a 4xx, a lapsed sign-in, a rate limit, a draft already gone — hands the card back. A failure that leaves it unclear — a timeout, a 5xx — leaves it `executing` and says to check the Sent folder, and the next scans ask Gmail: their message in the thread means it was sent; anything else is judged on the second scan that sees it: the draft still there and nothing sent means it was not (Gmail deletes a draft it sends), and the card comes back, flagged; the draft gone and nothing sent means it was deleted. Nothing is ever retried on its own. Sending is the person's own act, so it works while the Executive is paused.

### Limits and failures

At most 5 drafts a scan; `DELEGATION_INBOX_MAX_DRAFTS_PER_DAY` (default 20) a day, inside the shared `DELEGATION_MAX_DRAFTS_PER_DAY` it shares with chat; 200 classifications, 2 drafts per sender (1 for a stranger) and 10 for strangers in all per day; and never more than 25 open cards. A lapsed Gmail sign-in sets the status and is looked at again every 30 minutes; a rate limit, an error reaching Gmail or a crash backs off from 5 minutes, doubling up to 2 hours. Neither turns the switch off: the Settings card shows the status in plain words.

## Handle it for me

A third switch under Act as me, **Handle it for me** (`delegation.handle_it`), lets the inbox watcher send some of its replies itself instead of leaving them on a card. It is one row per person in `delegation_handle_it` (`enabled`, `mode`); no row means off. One setting says how much goes without them, the way quality does on the Agent Council (`handle_it.RULES`): **Easy ones** (`careful`) sends only replies to people they know (someone on their team, a contact or someone they have written to) of at most 400 characters when the classifier is at least 0.9 sure; **People I know** (`balanced`), where it starts, sends replies to people they know up to 1200 characters at 0.8; **Most mail** (`bold`) also answers strangers, up to 2000 characters, and lets a link or an amount through when the classifier is at least 0.9 sure. Everything else waits on a card as before, so turning it on never drafts less. A table from before the setting gets the `mode` column on its next open (`schema._add_handle_it_mode`): someone who had strangers set to send keeps that as Bold, everyone else gets Balanced. Only the person turns it on (`PUT /delegation/handle-it`), from a session the API knows is theirs: the same rule Send uses (`delegation.verified.caller_refusal`), so with only the shared secret it answers 409 `caller_signing_required`. Turning it on needs Act as me and Draft replies to my inbox on, and turning the inbox watcher off (or Act as me, which turns it off) turns it off too.

**In training** (`delegation.training`). Like someone new, each Act as me job can be put in training on its own, from that job's card on the Act as me page, the way Take the lead has it: **Write drafts as me** and **Handle it for me** each pick Off / In training / On (Handle it's In training puts Replies and Follow-ups in training together; its steps show under On only, since in training only allowed people go whatever the step), and **Suggested actions** picks Always ask / In training / On (On is the `actions_on` switch: a card is carried out with no allow, under the same checks, and only when it reaches nobody new: a new contact or anyone on the roster under a week waits; In training wins when both are set); what it learned is listed on each tab for its own jobs (Act as me: *What it's learned*, drafts and suggested actions; Handle it for me: *Who it's allowed to handle*, replies and follow-ups), each item named by its job (`PUT /delegation/training`, one row per person and setting in `delegation_training`, absent means not in training). In training it asks first and learns who and how from what the person approves; what it learns is a `take_the_lead_allowed` row (feature `act_as_me`, the person's id), theirs alone.

- **Replies.** Every reply waits on its card (`handle_it_reason` `training`) whatever the dial says, and a reply card adds **Send + allow**: it sends that reply on the person's own tap, exactly as Send does, then allows replies to that sender (key `act_as_me|person:<id>|reply|<address>`). While Handle it for me is on, a reply to an allowed sender goes on its own under the dial's limits (a stranger they allowed included) and every check above (the topics that always wait, links and amounts, new recipients, once a thread a day, the daily limit); it's checked again at send time, so a sender removed since waits. Take the lead as you lifts nothing in training: putting Replies or Follow-ups in training turns it off, and it can't be turned on while they are (409 `in_training`).
- **Follow-ups.** Every follow-up waits (`follow_up_training`); Send + allow on a follow-up card allows follow-ups to exactly the people it went to (`…|follow_up|<sorted addresses>`), whoever they are, under every other follow-up check.
- **Suggested actions.** An action card (below) adds **Approve + allow**: it does the actions on the tap, then allows each one that happened (a message to that person, `…|message|person:<id>`; a meeting with exactly those people, the person left out, `…|invite|people:<ids>`). A new contact is never allowed. A card proposed later whose every action is allowed is carried out at once, with no tap (`action_cards.run_on_its_own`, `gate_mode` `auto_execute`, status `executed`), only if plain code finds nothing against it (`on_its_own_refusal`): still in training, Act as me on, a server that ties the switch to the person, nothing sensitive, no link or amount, a message of at most 1200 characters, and at most 10 actions carried out this way a day (checked one card at a time); anything refused is handed back to wait on its card as before. An invite carried out this way is never booked as approved by the person: the meeting gate decides as for any meeting nobody tapped, so a time taken from someone's mail can't land on a calendar unasked. The tool result and chip say what was done. The message text in such an action is model-written from the mail and goes without anyone reading it; the allowance covers who and what kind, not the words, which is why sensitive topics, links, amounts and long messages are held back.
- **Drafts.** Nothing is sent. When the person changes a reply's draft in their mailbox before tapping Send (plain or + allow) and ticks **Do it like this next time**, what they sent is kept (its new text, quoted replies dropped, at most 1000 characters, `…|style|<address>`), and the ghostwriter gets it in its user turn as `<writer_example>` when it next writes to that person, from the inbox, a follow-up or a chat draft to that one person: style only, never its facts, and nothing in it can open or close a tag.

Send and Approve with the *on its own next time* tick (`allow`; the tick replaced the separate Send + allow and Approve + allow buttons) are refused before anything is done unless their setting is in training (422 `cant_allow`) and the person's list has room (409 `learned_full`, at most 200 a person); allowing failing afterwards never undoes the send. Putting Replies or Follow-ups in, or Suggested actions out of training or On, only holds more back and works without signed sign-ins; anything else needs a caller the API knows is that person. What it learned is the person's alone: listed on `GET /delegation` (`training.learned`, each with its `setting`), removed with `DELETE /delegation/learned/{id}`, and for the owner also in Take the lead's "What it's learned" list; it never reaches anyone else's list or Take the lead's prompts. A dial left on In training by an older version (mode `training`) moves to People I know with Replies and Follow-ups in training (`schema._move_training_off_the_dial`).

**No model decides whether a reply goes.** The watcher's two model calls are unchanged and tool-less, so text in an email can at most change the verdict and the draft. After the draft is written, `handle_it.refusal` — plain code — decides, and anything it refuses becomes the usual card with the reason kept on it (`handle_it_reason`). It refuses when:

- it's off, or the sender is a stranger and the setting isn't Bold, or on a server signed sign-ins are off (`signing_ok`: signed callers, or local login);
- Gmail couldn't authenticate the sender, whatever the roster says;
- the email isn't a question, request, scheduling, introduction or follow-up, or the classifier was less sure than the setting needs (0.9 on Easy ones, 0.8 otherwise);
- the reply goes to anyone the email didn't already go to (its From, To and Cc, less the person's own and the Executive's addresses), leaves out the sender, or goes to more than 10;
- the email's subject, the sender's new words, or the reply touch money, contracts, legal, hiring, pay, layoffs, the board, investors, mergers, the press, health, or credentials and secrets (passwords, logins, tokens, API keys); or the reply carries an amount, a percentage or a link (a scheme, `www.`, a bare host with a path such as `bit.ly/…`, or a bare host on a common top-level domain) unless it's Bold and at least 0.9 sure, or runs over the setting's length (400, 1200 or 2000 characters);
- the draft carries any flag but *others on the thread* or *Executive on the thread* (they asked if it's an AI, recipients were trimmed, …);
- it already sent one in this thread in the last day, or the person's last message in the thread was itself sent on its own (no auto-reply ping-pong);
- the day's limit is reached (`DELEGATION_HANDLE_IT_MAX_SENDS_PER_DAY`, default 20, within the watcher's drafts limit), or it can't be counted. Any error in the rules counts as a refusal.

**Workflows that email as their creator** (`delegation.workflow_email`). A workflow step can write an email in its creator's voice with `oe__draft_email_as_me` (a draft in their mailbox for them to send, counted and named in the briefs like a chat draft) or `oe__send_email_as_me` (sent). Which one a step lists is the choice the creator makes when they save it; the gateway's mail tools still send from the Executive's own address. Both write only as the workflow's creator (`dynamic_store.get_owner`), never an address the step names, and refuse a run someone else started by hand, a speaker the roster can't place, a run one of the Executive's own unattended passes started (reflection, research, a proactive run: `chat_tools.started_by_a_pass`, inherited by nested workflows), or a run another person's workflow started (`chat_tools.running`); a scheduled run writes as the creator. The creator must be allowed Act as me, have it on and have their own mailbox connected, or the step is told to use the Executive's own email. `to` and `cc` are write targets (`action_step.TargetPolicy`). The creator's own addresses and the addresses in the saved goal of a step that emails as them, nowhere else in the workflow (`workflow_email.chosen_recipients`; only its verified creator saves one, and a definition that differs from the saved copy gets none) go without asking; the first email to any other address waits for the creator's approval and is then remembered. Every email counts against `DELEGATION_MAX_DRAFTS_PER_DAY`, and sends against `DELEGATION_WORKFLOW_MAX_SENDS_PER_DAY` (default 20) as well, counted from `delegation_drafts` rows with source `workflow_sent` (written before the send, so a failed send still counts). Sending needs more: a workflow with `oe__send_email_as_me` can only be created, changed or switched on by its creator from a session the API knows is theirs (`workflow_email.save_refusal`, the `verified.caller_refusal` rule Send uses; a 403 otherwise, from `POST`/`PUT /workflows/custom`, save-edit and activate), and chat's `save_workflow` never replaces one, so nobody else can change what it sends. At send time `reply_send.send_for_workflow` checks again that Act as me is on, `handle_it.signing_ok`, no client slot is active, and the draft it just wrote is unchanged: addressed exactly as written, from one of their own addresses, at most 10 recipients and never the Executive's own address. A send the mailbox didn't confirm is reported as possibly sent and never retried. The step's result (and so the run's report) names who it went to and the subject, never the body; the audit rows (`delegation_drafted`, `delegation_workflow_sent`, `delegation_workflow_send_refused`) are the creator's alone. The workflow designer is told whether the person designing it can have email written as them, and to ask when it isn't clear whether an email should come from them or from the Executive.

**Workflows that read their creator's mail** (`delegation.workflow_reads`). A step may also read the creator's own mailbox and calendar with `oe__search_my_email`, `oe__read_my_email`, `oe__my_email_awaiting_reply` and `oe__my_calendar`: chat's own reads (`mail_read_tools`), run as the workflow's creator through `AS_CREATOR` in place of the chat turn's speaker, with the same per-call caps and the same untrusted-content marking. They read only on a run that is the creator's: started by them by hand (`turn_owner` is them) or by its schedule, and only in the outermost workflow (never one another workflow started, whose later steps would see the mail), never on a run an unattended pass, an inbound message or someone else started. Act as me must be allowed and on and the mailbox connected; `my_calendar` also needs Read my calendar on. Such a run is the creator's alone: the scheduler creates a scheduled run as theirs (`owner_person_id`, viewer pinned to them), delivers its report and any failure card to them whatever the cadence names, the run route returns 403 to anyone else, and every audit row the run writes (scheduled, from the Jobs page, from chat or resumed, its report's delivery included) is theirs alone, with no send on the shared activity rail (`workflow_reads.private_run`, `rows_for_person`). Chat's `run_workflow` starts one only for its creator on a turn Act as me was offered on, and first marks that turn as one that read their mail (private, and locked down for the rest of it), since the report comes back into it. The lockdown a chat turn gets after a read covers the whole workflow, checked when it is saved (`definition_refusal`, also in chat's `draft_workflow`/`save_workflow`) and at every step (`run_rules`): its steps may list only the reads, the email-as-them tools (`workflow_email.TOOLS`: a send goes without asking only to an address the creator chose, so mail text naming another address gets a card first) and chat tools in `MAIL_TOUCHED_ALLOWED_TOOLS` (no gateway, extension or web-search tool, no `run_workflow`, nothing that posts to everyone), get no `run_script`, and may have no approval gate asking anyone but the creator and no cadence reporting to anyone else. Like one that sends, a workflow that reads can only be created, changed or switched on by its verified creator (`workflow_email.save_refusal`).

A reply the rules allow gets a card with `gate_mode` `auto_execute`, and the watcher sends it at once through `reply_send.send_on_its_own`, the second door into the send path (an AST test pins its callers: the approve route, the watcher, and a workflow's `oe__send_email_as_me`). It runs the same send-time checks as a tap — switches, mailbox, draft, recipients, the claim and the last re-read — with no caller, and adds its own: the card must be `auto_execute`, Handle it for me still on with the setting still allowing that sender (or, for a follow-up, that recipient), signing still on, the once-a-thread-a-day rule and the daily limit counted again, and the draft untouched since it was saved (an edit in Gmail means the person has taken it over: `draft_changed`, the card waits for them). Every refusal hands the card back to the person (`decision_ledger.hand_back`, a compare-and-set to `propose`), with the reason kept on it when there are words for it, and a failure never stops the scan. Every card it left for the person says why on Today (`waited_because` on `GET /delegation/replies`). A reply sent on its own finishes as `executed` (not approved), is recorded in `delegation_handled` (for the per-thread and daily rules) and writes a private `delegation_reply_handled` row; an unconfirmed one is settled by the reconciler the same way. No History note is taken from it, since notes come only from the person's own words. It runs inside the watcher's scan, so it stops while the Executive is paused.

**Follow-ups as you** (`delegation.follow_ups`). While Handle it for me is on, the watcher's scan also looks at the person's own sent mail, at most once an hour (`LOOK_EVERY`), for an email of theirs that asked something (a question mark in their own words), is 3 to 10 days old, went to at most 10 people other than the Executive, and is still the last message in its thread. Plain code picks it; each gets one follow-up ever (its `delegation_inbox_messages` row), at most two a look, within the drafts limit. The ghostwriter, tool-less as always, writes a short nudge in their voice from the thread, saved as a draft in that thread to exactly the people the email went to. `handle_it.follow_up_refusal` — plain code — decides whether it goes: by the setting it never goes on Easy ones, goes to their team and contacts on People I know and to anyone they wrote to on Most mail (`follow_up_refused` otherwise: `follow_up_level`); it also refuses on any change of recipients, a sensitive topic, an amount or a link, more than 600 characters, a flag, and the same per-thread and daily counts as replies. It goes through `send_on_its_own` on an ordinary `delegation_reply` card marked `source: follow_up`, which rechecks the setting for that recipient. A refused one waits on Today as **Follow-up waiting**, and closes by itself (its untouched draft deleted) when anyone answers in the thread first.

**What it sent** is the person's alone: `GET /delegation/handled` lists the last 7 days (who, subject, the reply, the questions it left them and a link to the thread in their mailbox), and the Handle it for me tab shows it with how many went today, under its picker.

### Take the lead as you

On Settings → Act as me, Handle it for me is one dial: **Off**, **Easy ones**, **People I know**, **Most mail** and, for the owner, **Everything**, which uses **Take the lead** (`PUT /delegation/take-the-lead`, one row `person:<id>` in `take_the_lead`; turning it on turns Handle it for me on). While it is on, `handle_it.refusal` drops the setting's limits: strangers, the classifier's confidence, amounts, and the length up to a 4000-character ceiling. A reply with a link still waits for a tap (refusal `link`). In their place it checks the company's and the person's own added rules (`take_the_lead.reply_hit`, refusal `lead_rule`). Everything Handle it always keeps still holds: signed sign-ins, an authenticated sender, a reply kind, exactly the thread's people, the topics that always wait, draft flags, never twice in a row, one a thread a day and the daily limit. Follow-ups under it may go to anyone the person wrote to, with the same sensitive, amount, link and length checks plus the added rules. `reply_send.send_on_its_own` accepts the card while both switches are on. Each person adds and removes their own rules (`/delegation/take-the-lead/rules`). Removing one needs a caller the API can tie to them.


## Meeting invites

With **Read my calendar** on, a calendar invite in the person's inbox no longer just gets skipped (`delegation.invites`). The watcher applies its usual rules, less the ones about writing a reply (a calendar service's own Sender header doesn't make it automatic; a big meeting isn't too many recipients), and then looks at who sent it: someone the person knows — their team, a contact, or someone they have written to (`inbox.relation_of`), with the sender confirmed by the mail service (`inbox.handling_relation`) — or it is skipped as `invite_stranger` / `invite_unverified`. It then finds the event on their own calendar: on Google by the invite's iCalendar UID (read from its `text/calendar` part, or its attached `.ics`) in their primary calendar, on Outlook as the invite message's own event; only a request counts (a cancellation or someone's answer doesn't). An event that can't be found, isn't organized by the sender, is already answered or has already started is skipped with that reason, as before. **No model is called** for an invite.

What's left becomes a card, a `delegation_invite` decision that is its person's alone (`approver_only`) and never an alert, like a reply card: who invited them, the title, when (in the workspace time zone) and any **clash** — the busy times on their calendar that overlap the meeting, computed in code from the calendar read; only start and end times reach the card, never another event's title. **Accept** and **Decline** are `POST /decisions/{id}/approve` with `edits.answer` (`accept`, the default, or `decline`), on the same caller checks Send uses (`verified.caller_refusal`); the card is claimed, then answered with the mailbox client's `answer_invite`. Answering again is harmless, so a failure releases the card for another try; an event that has gone fails it. **Dismiss** (`reject`) answers nothing. A sign-in that reads but can't write the calendar keeps its card, which says to connect again under Read my calendar (with the command) instead of offering Accept. A card closes by itself once the meeting starts or after a week, and its thread waits until it's settled.

**On its own.** Under Handle it for me (On, or Take the lead as you) it accepts with no tap when plain code finds nothing against it (`invites.refusal`): a sender on their team or in their contacts, never one known only from their Sent mail (with Replies in training, only one they ticked **Accept from them on its own next time** for), signed sign-ins or local login, no clash and a calendar it could read, nothing sensitive in the title, a sign-in that can answer, and Handle it for me's daily limit and once-a-day-per-thread rule (`handle_it.count_refusal`, `record_handled`). It never declines on its own. Anything against it leaves the usual card saying why. An accepted invite is listed with the replies it sent: `GET /delegation/handled` (`source: invite`, with a one-line `summary` such as "Accepted Dana's Pilot review, Wed 21 Oct, 14:30") and Today's `sent_as_you` activity, the person's alone.

**In training.** With Replies in training, a card has the same tick as a reply card; ticking it and tapping Accept adds `Accept invites from <name>` to their learned list (key `act_as_me|person:<id>|invite_from|<address>`, under Replies), removable like any other.

Audit rows, all private to the person: `delegation_invite_carded`, `delegation_invite_answered`, `delegation_invite_handled`, `delegation_invite_dismissed`.

## AI line on replies

Replies written as a person can end with **"Drafted and sent by my AI assistant."** (`delegation.disclosure.LINE`), by two switches that are each person's own (`PUT /delegation/disclosure`, one row per person in `delegation_disclosure`, NULL following the install): **Handle it**, on by default (`AI_DISCLOSURE_HANDLE_IT`), for a reply Handle it for me will send on its own, which nobody reads before it goes; and **Approved sends**, off by default (`AI_DISCLOSURE_APPROVED_SENDS`), for one that waits on a card for them to send, since they read it first. The line is written into the reply when it is drafted (`disclosure.sign`, in `inbox._consider` and `follow_ups`), once the plain-code checks have decided whether it goes on its own, so the card, the mailbox draft and what is sent are the same words and Send's draft-changed checks see them; a switch changed later applies to the next reply, and a reply drafted to go on its own that is handed back keeps its line for the person to edit. `AI_DISCLOSURE` off turns both off and hides the card. Turning a switch on only adds the line, so it needs no signed sign-in; turning one off does. Each tab shows its own switch under Advanced (**AI line on drafts you send** on Act as me, **AI line on replies it sends** on Handle it for me), and turning off the Handle it line asks first.

## The mailbox client

`delegation.gmail.DelegateGmail` talks to the Gmail REST API directly and is **never registered with the MCP gateway**, so the model reaches the mailbox only through the typed handler. The credential is one file per person in `DELEGATION_GOOGLE_CREDENTIALS_DIR`, named from a hash of the address (0600 in a 0700 directory), minted by `scripts/connect-own-gmail.py` on the Executive's own OAuth client with the scopes `gmail.readonly` and `gmail.compose`. It never lives in `WORKSPACE_MCP_CREDENTIALS_DIR`, where workspace-mcp picks a credential by address. Besides reading threads and saving drafts it lists the inbox and checks whether they have written to an address, reads one message or draft, lists the person's send-as addresses and deletes a draft. Its **one send method**, `send_draft`, sends an existing draft by its id and nothing else — never `messages.send`, which sends any text it is given — and unit tests pin the method set, the endpoint, the request body and its single caller. On the calendar it reads (`list_events`, `find_invite`: an invite's event by its iCalendar UID) and makes one change, `answer_invite`: the person's own attendee answer on one event, with `sendUpdates=all` so the organizer hears (`calendar_write_granted` says whether the sign-in allows it; a read-only one raises `CalendarWriteNotGranted`). A failed request says whether it may have been carried out anyway (a timeout after connecting, a 5xx), which is what the send path needs to know. A parsed message carries when it arrived, whether it is bulk, a bounce or a calendar invite, and whether Gmail's authentication results vouch for its sender.

`gmail_status` answers `connected`, `not_configured`, `needs_reconnect` (Google refused the saved sign-in — an app in Testing mode has its tokens expire after 7 days; a rate limit, though Gmail may send it as a 403, is an `error` to retry, not a reconnect), `mismatch`, `no_email`, `shared_mailbox` or `error`. `shared_mailbox` means the person's address *is* the Executive's; it is refused before asking Google, because then everything the Executive writes would look like theirs. The gateway closes the other door: every `google_workspace__*` call must act as the Executive's own account, and a `user_google_email` naming anyone else is refused and audited (see Integrations).

### Outlook

A person may connect an Outlook mailbox instead (work, school or personal), with `scripts/connect-own-outlook.py`: a device-code sign-in on the Executive's own Entra app (`MS365_MCP_CLIENT_ID`, tenant `MS365_MCP_TENANT_ID` or `common`) asking for `User.Read`, `Mail.ReadWrite`, `Mail.Send` and `offline_access` (and `Calendars.ReadWrite` with `--calendar`; an invite is the invite message's own `eventMessage.event`, answered with Graph's event `accept` or `decline` and `sendResponse`). It writes the same per-person file with `"provider": "microsoft"`, so a person has one mailbox for Act as me, and `gmail_for` hands back `delegation.outlook.DelegateOutlook`, which keeps `DelegateGmail`'s methods, return types and errors, so every caller above runs unchanged. It talks to Microsoft Graph directly, never through the Microsoft 365 MCP server the Executive's own Outlook uses, and is never registered with the gateway. Microsoft rotates the refresh token on use; the new one is written back into the file (atomically, keeping every other key, and only if the file still holds the old one). Graph is asked for immutable ids, so a sent draft keeps its id; a thread is Outlook's `conversationId`. Gmail's labels are mapped onto what the callers read: `SENT` only for mail in their Sent Items folder (a From line set to their address by someone else never counts), `DRAFT`, `INBOX`, and Focused Inbox's Other read as a tab. A sender counts as authenticated only when the topmost `Authentication-Results` — the one Exchange wrote, above anything the sender added — holds exactly one DMARC verdict, a pass for From's own domain, and Exchange Online Protection's own `compauth=` verdict, so a header the sender wrote on mail EOP never stamped doesn't count. `delete_draft` refuses anything that isn't a draft, and deletes with the draft's etag (`If-Match`), so a draft sent in between — it keeps its id — is left alone. No client secret is ever written into a person's file, and Graph has no signature setting to read.

## Privacy

What a person's mailbox touches is theirs. For the principal that means private to the principal, as every private row is. For a team member it means theirs alone, the principal included: an audit row carries `private_to_person` (set by `audit.rows_for_person` around the inbox watcher, a card's Send and Dismiss and their settings changes, and by `people_tools.audit_row_owner` on a turn that read their mail) and is left out of every audit read — the log, a session's timeline, a row by id, the brief — with only the usage totals counting it; their reply cards are theirs alone (above); and the owner's view of their use is counts only (drafts and sends in 30 days, and whether their inbox watcher is on). The conversation itself becomes its owner's alone before the mailbox is first read: `ghostwrite_email` marks the session `mail_private` (`session_store.mark_mail_private`, creating a channel adapter's row early, with its owner) and refuses to read the mailbox if that can't be stored or the conversation already belongs to someone else (which it then leaves unmarked); from then on only its owner may open it (`chat._session_access`), and working-style learning skips it. Every later turn there starts private (`settings.pin_turn_delegation` reads the flag and fails closed, setting `touched_mail`), so a follow-up answered from history alone is still private to its owner and teaches no memory, and the web chat's rows before the turn (the inbound message and the knowledge lookup) are theirs too. It does not start locked down: the lockdown is `read_mail`, set only by a turn that reads the mailbox or notes itself, and it is never carried into the next turn, because history keeps only the speaker's words and the Executive's replies, never the mail a tool returned. Their next message is them asking again, having read that reply, so everything runs again there. Anyone else speaking in it is not offered Act as me.

Once `touched_mail` is set, every audit row the turn writes is private (`people_tools.audit_row_private_to_principal`), and a team member's is theirs alone: the tool row (its input and result redacted, since `ghostwrite` is a sensitive tool name), the reply's `chat_turn` row that carries the preview, the model-call rows, and the background passes, which run under `private_rows`. The Honcho peer and department syncs are skipped, because peer memory is read on other people's turns. No memory is learned from the turn at all: the episodic, open-loop and working-style passes are skipped too, since its reply quotes a draft built from other people's mail. The `delegation_*` audit events are always private and carry metadata only — ids, counts and flags, never the draft or the thread. The inbox watcher is private the same way: every row a scan or a card action writes is its person's alone, and it starts no chat turn, alert, scheduled action or workflow run and teaches no memory.

The turn also keeps one door shut (`delegation.lockdown`). Anyone can put text in the inbox, and that text could try to steer the model, so from the round that calls `ghostwrite_email` or one of the mailbox reads — a round's tools run together — until the turn ends, the dispatch guard refuses only what opens the open internet or reaches everyone: outside fetches (`read_document`, research, the watchlist, `load_mcp_server`, and any MCP `call_tool` outside the private-turn set of reads and recipient-checked sends), `run_script` and `run_python_job`, workflows (they run later, unattended, and may fetch or script), broadcasts, department messages and alerts, and changes to who is on the roster or holds authority (`archive_person`, `set_department_head`, `resolve_roster_request`), and text that steers later turns (`schedule_followup`, whose intent runs unattended when due, and goals and decision outcomes, shown to every later turn).
